The history of science provides strong empirical grounding for the view that scientific knowledge is best understood as provisional and fallible rather than as a corpus of established certainties. Major episodes in the development of science show that even theories once regarded as paradigmatic successes were later revised, restricted, or replaced in light of new empirical and theoretical developments. Newtonian mechanics, for example, achieved extraordinary predictive success across a vast range of terrestrial and celestial phenomena and was long treated as a nearly complete description of motion and gravitation. Yet the emergence of relativistic physics and quantum theory revealed that Newtonian mechanics holds only within bounded domains, namely regimes of low velocity and weak gravitational fields, and is not universally valid. Similarly, classical thermodynamics offered a deeply successful framework for macroscopic systems, but its scope was shown to be limited when statistical mechanics and later developments in quantum theory provided more fundamental accounts of entropy and microphysical behavior. These episodes do not merely illustrate refinement within stable foundations; they demonstrate systematic revision of what were previously taken to be fundamental laws. The most empirically warranted epistemic stance, therefore, is fallibilism: the recognition that scientific theories are always subject to correction, restriction, or replacement as inquiry progresses and as new domains of phenomena become accessible.

The Duhem–Quine thesis further supports the view that scientific knowledge is inherently provisional by showing that individual hypotheses cannot be tested in isolation from a wider theoretical network. Any empirical test depends not only on the target hypothesis but also on a background set of auxiliary assumptions concerning measurement devices, initial conditions, and the relevant auxiliary theories that connect observation to prediction. When an experiment yields a result inconsistent with prediction, logic alone does not determine which component of the broader theoretical system is at fault; the anomalous outcome can be accommodated by revising the core hypothesis, adjusting auxiliary assumptions, or modifying background theories. As a result, experimental falsification is never uniquely directed at a single proposition but instead affects an interconnected web of commitments. Scientific knowledge is therefore irreducibly holistic, in the sense that its components are mutually dependent within a network of inferential relations, and defeasible, in that any element of the network can be retained by revising other parts to preserve overall coherence with the data.

The underdetermination of theory by evidence strengthens this conclusion by showing that empirical data alone cannot uniquely determine which of multiple competing theoretical frameworks is correct. For any finite body of observational data, there exist multiple logically distinct theories that are compatible with that data while differing in their underlying ontological commitments, explanatory structures, or unobservable posits. Because empirical evidence is always finite and theory space is potentially infinite, no amount of available data can conclusively rule out all alternative theoretical formulations that match the observed outcomes. Consequently, empirical confirmation is inherently partial, providing support for theories relative to their rivals rather than yielding absolute certainty. Claims of definitive or final justification therefore exceed what the evidential basis can support, since the same data can be embedded within distinct theoretical frameworks that diverge in unobserved but scientifically meaningful ways.
